verses.text: Solomon son of David became firmly in control of his kingdom. Yahweh his God helped him and made him a very great king.

Solomon called together many Israelite leaders, including the officers who commanded groups of a thousand soldiers and groups of a hundred soldiers. He also called together the judges and other leaders in Israel who governed clans.

Solomon and all those leaders went together to the hilltop shrine at Gibeon. They went there because God’s sacred tent was there. Moses, Yahweh’s servant, had made that tent while the Israelites were traveling through the desolate area between Egypt and Canaan.

Now the sacred chest was no longer there because David and the Israelite leaders had brought it from the city of Kiriath Jearim to Jerusalem. David had prepared a place for it by setting up a tent for it.

However, the bronze altar that Bezalel had made was still at Gibeon. Bezalel was the son of Uri and the grandson of Hur. That altar was in front of the sacred tent. So Solomon and the Israelite leaders prayed to Yahweh there.
So Solomon went to the bronze altar in front of the sacred tent, where Yahweh was present. He offered a thousand animals as sacrifices that the priests burned completely on the altar.
That night, God appeared to Solomon {in a dream}. He told him, “Tell me what you want, and I will give it to you.”
Solomon replied to God, “You always loved my father David very faithfully, and now you have made me the next king of Israel.

Yahweh my God, you have made me the king of a nation that has very many people, just as there is very much dust on the earth. So please do what you promised to my father David {and make me a successful king}.
Please enable me to be wise and to know what I should do. Then I will be able to rule these people well. Otherwise, I would not be able to rule this great nation of yours.”

God replied to Solomon, “You did not ask to become very rich or famous. You did not ask that would you be able to kill your enemies. You also did not ask to live for a long time. Instead, you asked me to make you wise and help you know what to do. Then you would be able to decide fairly the cases of the people whose king I have made you. Because that is what you wanted,
I will make you wise and help you know what to do. But I will also make you very rich and famous, more than any king was before you or will be after you.”
Then Solomon and the leaders who were with him left the sacred tent that was at the hilltop shrine in Gibeon. They returned to Jerusalem, and from there Solomon ruled the Israelite people.

Solomon acquired a great force of chariots and riders. In his army, he had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 men who rode on horses. Solomon had built special cities in which to keep chariots, and he kept many of his chariots in them. But he also kept some chariots with him in Jerusalem.

During the years that Solomon was king, silver and gold became very common in Jerusalem, just as stones are common. Cedar wood became very plentiful, just as the wood is plentiful that comes from the sycamore trees that grow in the foothills of Judah.
Solomon imported his horses from Egypt and Kue. His purchasing agents would go to Kue and buy horses there at the current price.

In Egypt, his agents bought both horses and chariots. They paid about seven kilograms of silver for each chariot and about two kilograms of silver for each horse. Agents of Solomon would then resell many of the horses and chariots to Hittite and Aramean kings.
Solomon decided to build a temple to honor Yahweh and a royal palace.
He required Israelite men to become his workers. 70,000 of them would carry heavy loads. 80,000 of them would cut stones from quarries in the hills. 3,600 other men would supervise them.
Solomon sent this message to King Hiram of the city of Tyre: “When my father David was building a palace to live in, you sent him cedar logs. Please do the same for me.

I ask this because I am going to build a temple to honor Yahweh my God. It will be a special place where we will worship him. We will burn fragrant spices as incense to him. Our priests will put fresh bread in rows on a special table every week. They will burn sacrifices completely on an altar every morning and evening. They will also do that on Sabbath days, on New Moon festivals, and at each of the feasts that we celebrate each year to honor Yahweh our God. We Israelites must always do these things.
The temple that I am going to build must be a very great temple, because our God is greater than all other gods.

(But no one is really able to build a place for God to live in, since the whole sky and the spiritual realm beyond the sky are not big enough for him. I myself do not deserve to build a temple for him except as a place to offer sacrifices to him.)

So please send me someone who can make things expertly from gold, silver, bronze, and iron. He should also be able to make things expertly from purple, red, and blue cloth. He should also be able to carve designs in wood very skillfully. I want him to work here in Jerusalem and in other places in Judah with the skilled craftsmen whom my father David trained.

I know that your workers are able very skillfully to cut down the great trees that grow in Lebanon. So please also send me cedar logs, cypress logs, and algum logs from there. My workers will work together with your workers.
In that way, they will be able to provide me with much lumber. We will need much because the temple that I am going to build will be large and beautiful.
I will agree to pay your workers, the men who cut the logs, 4,400 kiloliters of ground wheat, 4,400 kiloliters of barley, 440 kiloliters of wine, and 440 kiloliters of olive oil.”
King Hiram of Tyre responded by sending a letter to Solomon. He wrote, “Yahweh has made you the king of his people because he loves them.

He also wrote, “I thank Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, who created the sky and the land, for giving King David such a wise and intelligent son! He will build a temple for Yahweh and a royal palace.
I agree to send you Huram Abi, one of my skilled craftsmen.

His mother was {an Israelite} from the tribe of Dan, and his father was from here in Tyre. He is able to make things expertly from gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood. He is also able to make things expertly from purple, blue, linen, and red cloth. He is able to carve various designs in wood very skillfully. He can make things using any design that you give to him. He will work with your craftsmen and with the craftsmen who worked for your father, King David.
Now please send us the wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine that you promised to send to us.

My workers will cut from the mountains in Lebanon all the logs that you need. They will bring the logs to you by tying them together to form rafts and floating them by sea to the city of Joppa. From there, your workers can bring them to Jerusalem.”
Solomon had his servants count all the men from other countries who were living in Israel, just as his father David had done. There were 153,600 of them.
Solomon required 70,000 of them to carry heavy loads and 80,000 of them to cut stones from quarries in the hills. He appointed 3,600 other men to supervise them so that they would work steadily.

Then Solomon’s workers started to build a temple for Yahweh in Jerusalem. They built it on Mount Moriah, where Yahweh had appeared to Solomon’s father David. They built it at the place where Araunah the Jebusite used to thresh his grain. David had chosen that place as the site for the temple.
They started the work on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign.
The foundation of the temple that Solomon was building for God was about twenty-seven meters long and about nine meters wide.

There was a porch in front of the temple that went across its entire width, so it was also about nine meters wide. This porch was about nine meters high. The workers covered the interior walls of the temple with very thin sheets of pure gold.

Solomon’s workers paneled the walls of the main hall of the temple with cypress wood. They decorated the panels with carvings of palm trees and chains. They covered the panels with very thin sheets of pure gold.
The workers decorated the temple with gemstones to make it beautiful. The gold that they used came from the land of Parvaim.
They covered the ceiling beams, doorframes, walls and doors of the temple with very thin sheets of gold. They decorated the walls with artistic carvings of winged creatures.

The workers built a room inside the temple to be the Most Holy Place. This room went all the way across the temple building, so it was about nine meters wide, and it extended out nine meters from the back wall of the temple. The workers covered its walls with very thin sheets of pure gold. Altogether this gold weighed about twenty metric tons.
They used gold nails that weighed about half a kilogram. There were upper rooms in the temple, and the workers also covered their walls with very thin sheets of gold.
Solomon’s workers made wooden statues of two winged creatures to put inside the Most Holy Place. They covered them with very thin sheets of gold.

Each creature had two wings. Each wing was about two and one third meters long, so the total length of all the wings was about nine meters. The workers arranged the statues so that each of the creatures’ outer wings touched a side wall of the room and their inner wings touched each other.
So the wings of these creatures extended all the way across the room, a distance of about nine meters. The creatures were standing up and facing the doorway leading to the main hall of the temple.
Solomon’s workers made a curtain {to separate the main hall from the Most Holy Place}. They wove it from blue, purple, red, and linen thread. They wove figures of winged creatures into the curtain.
Huram Abi made two bronze pillars for the entrance to the temple. Their combined length was nearly 17 meters. Each pillar had a decorative top that was two and one third meters high.
Huram made bronze chains like the ones inside the temple and put them on the decorative tops of the pillars. He made 100 bronze pomegranates for each pillar and attached them to the chains.

Solomon”s workers set up the pillars in front of the temple. One was on the south side of the entrance and the other was on the north side. Solomon named the one on the south side Jakin, and he named the one on the north side Boaz.
Solomon’s workers made a bronze altar. It was nine meters wide, nine meters deep, and four and and a half meters high.

Huram Abi made a giant water basin. People called it a sea {because it contained so much water}. Huram made it by casting bronze in a clay mold. This sea was four and a half meters across its circular top, two and one third meters tall, and nearly 14 meters around.

All around the outer edge of the sea there were decorations in the shape of oxen. There were two rows of oxen. There were ten oxen for every 45 centimeters of the outer edge. Hiram included the oxen as part of the design of the sea when he cast it.

Hiram cast 12 bronze statues of oxen to be a stand for the sea. He placed the oxen in groups of three facing outward to the north, south, east, and west. Then workers put the sea on the statues of the oxen, and it covered their backs.

The sides of this large water basin were eight centimeters thick. When Hiram cast the basin, he made the rim curve outward, like the rim of a cup and like the petals of a lily. The basin could hold over 60,000 liters of water.

Huram also made ten basins. Solomon’s workers put five of these basins on the south side of the temple and five of them on the north side of the temple. They were for rinsing the parts of the animals that the priests burned completely on the altar as sacrifices. But the priests washed their hands and feet {to become ritually clean when they came to the temple} in the large water basin that people called a sea.

Huram also made ten gold lampstands in the same shape in which God had told Moses to make lampstands for the sacred tent. He put five of these lampstands on the south side in the temple and five of them on the north side of the temple.
Huram also made ten tables. He put five of them on the south side of the temple and five of them on the north side of the temple. He also made 100 gold basins.

Solomon’s workers constructed a courtyard for the priests and a larger court area for other Israelites. They made doors for the entrances to these courtyards, and they covered the doors with thin sheets of bronze.
Solomon’s workers put the giant water basin that people called a sea by the southeast corner of the temple.
Huram also made {bronze} pots {in which to boil meat}, shovels {for removing ashes}, and bowls {to catch the blood of the animals that the priests sacrificed}.
{What Huram made included} the two pillars {for the temple porch}, the two ball-shaped tops for the pillars, the two bronze nets that decorated the ball-shaped pillar tops,
the 400 bronze pomegranates that decorated the two networks (these pomegranates were in two rows around each bronze net, and they covered the round lower parts of the pillar tops),
ten carts and ten basins that the carts held,
the giant water basin that people called the sea, the 12 statues of oxen on whose backs the sea rested,
as well as pots, shovels, and meat forks.

Hiram and his workers made these things for Solomon in the Jordan River valley, between the cities of Succoth and Zaredathah. {They made them there because} the soil consisted of clay {that they could use to cast things in bronze}.
Because Huram used so much bronze to make all these objects for Solomon, Solomon did not command his workers to weigh them. So no one ever knew what they weighed.
Solomon’s workers also made all the gold items that the priests needed to use in Yahweh’s temple. They made the golden altar and the table that held the sacred bread.

They made from pure gold the lampstands and the lamps they held. They put the lampstands in front of the Most Holy Place. The priests kept those lamps burning all night long, as God had told Moses they should do.
They also made decorations for the lampstands that looked like flowers, the lamps themselves, and tongs {for removing burnt parts of the lamp wicks}. They made all of these articles from solid gold.

Solomon’s workers also made from pure gold the wick snuffers, small bowls, incense dishes, and pans for carrying hot coals {that the priests used in the temple}. They also made golden sockets for the doors of the temple building and for the doors inside the building that led into the Most Holy Place.
So Solomon’s workers finished all the work for Yahweh’s temple. Then Solomon put the silver and gold and other valuable items that his father David had dedicated to Yahweh in the temple storerooms.

Solomon then sent messengers to tell the Israelite elders, tribal leaders, and clan leaders to come to Jerusalem. He wanted them to join him in a ceremony to move Yahweh’s sacred chest from the City of David (the part of Jerusalem that people now call Zion) {into the temple that he had built}.

King Solomon asked the leaders to come during the Festival of Shelters, which the Israelites observed in the seventh month of the year. So a very large crowd of Israelites also came to Jerusalem at that time to celebrate this festival.
When the Israelite leaders had all arrived, the Levites carried the sacred chest {from the City of David}
and brought it into the temple. The Levites {who assisted the priests} helped them carry into the temple the sacred tent and all the special equipment that the priests used only in the tent.

King Solomon and that large crowd of Israelites walked together ahead of Yahweh’s sacred chest {as the priests carried it to the temple}. They sacrificed a very large number of sheep and bulls. No one was able to count how many animals they sacrificed, because there were so many.

The priests carried the sacred chest into the temple and put it where it belonged. That was in the Most Holy Place, the special room that Solomon’s workers had made at the back of the temple. They placed the sacred chest under the wings of the statues of the winged creatures there.
Then the wings of those statues extended over the sacred chest and over the poles that the priests used to carry it.

Those poles were so long that priests who were standing in the Holy Place at the entrance to the Most Holy Place could see their ends. But people standing outside the temple could not see them. Those poles are still there.

The only things that were in the sacred chest were the two stone tablets that Moses had put there at Mount Horeb. That was where Yahweh had made a special agreement with the Israelites after they left Egypt.

Then the priests came out of the Holy Place{, after putting the sacred chest in the temple}. All the priests who were there had made themselves ritually clean, not just the ones from the group that was officially on duty that day.)

The Levites who were musicians—Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and other relatives—were standing on the east side of the altar. They were wearing linen clothes, and they were playing cymbals, lyres, and harps. There were 120 priests with them who were playing trumpets.

On their trumpets, the priests were accompanying the tune that the singers were singing. They were all praising and thanking Yahweh. The priests were playing their trumpets, and others were sounding cymbals and playing other musical instruments, as the Levites praised Yahweh by singing, “He always does good things for us, and he will love us faithfully forever!”
The glorious presence of Yahweh, which the cloud expressed, filled the temple. As a result, the priests were not able to continue their work.
Then Solomon {looked at the temple and} said, “Yahweh said that he would live in a dark cloud.”
{Then Solomon prayed to Yahweh,} “But I have built a temple for you that you will always be able to live in.”
Then, while all the people stood there {respectfully}, the king turned around and faced them, and he asked God to make good things happen for them.
Then he said, “Praise Yahweh, the God whom we Israelites worship! By his own power he has done what he promised to my father David. Yahweh told him,

‘I rescued the people who belong to me from slavery in Egypt. But right after that, I did not choose a city anywhere in their land and ask them to build a temple there where they would worship me. I also did not choose a man to be the king of my Israelite people.
But now I have chosen Jerusalem as the place where people will worship me, and I have chosen you, David, to be the king of my Israelite people.’”
Then Solomon said, “My father David wanted very much to build a temple where we Israelite people could worship Yahweh our God.
But Yahweh told him, ‘You wanted to build a temple for me, and it was good that you wanted to do that.
However, you are not the one who is going to build it. Instead, one of your own sons will build a temple where the Israelites will worship me.’

And now Yahweh has done what he promised to do. I have succeeded my father David as the king of Israel, just as Yahweh promised. And I have built a temple where we Israelite people can worship Yahweh our God.
I have provided a place within the temple for the sacred chest. It holds the two stone tablets that Moses put in it when Yahweh made a special agreement with our ancestors.”

Then Solomon turned around again and faced the altar {in the temple courtyard}. The Israelite people who had gathered for this occasion could see and hear him. He lifted his hands toward the sky {to pray}.

Now Solomon’s workers had built a bronze platform for him. It was two and one third meters wide, two and one third meters deep, and one and a half meters high. They had put it in the courtyard outside the temple. Solomon had been standing on that platform, but then he knelt down in front of all the Israelites who had gathered there, and that was when he lifted his hands toward the sky.

Then he prayed, “Yahweh, you are the God whom we Israelite people worship. There is no god like you in heaven or on earth. You solemnly promised that you would faithfully love us. And that is what you have always done for us when we have earnestly done what you wanted us to do.
You promised my father David, who served you faithfully, that his son would build a temple for you. And we here today can all see that by your own power you have done what you promised.

So now, Yahweh, the God whom we Israelites worship, I am asking you to do the further things you promised to my father David, who served you faithfully. You told him that you would make sure that one of his descendants would always be the king of Israel if they would conduct their lives as he did. He obeyed you carefully.
You, Yahweh, are the God whom we Israelite people worship. So now please do what you promised to do for my father David.

But you, God, will not really live with people here on the earth. You are so great that the whole sky and even the spiritual realm beyond the sky are not a sufficient home for you. So this temple that I have built is certainly not sufficient for you to live in either.
Even so, Yahweh, my God, please grant the requests that I make as I pray to you today. I have come to your temple today to pray. Please do what I am earnestly asking you to do.

I pray that you will always regard this temple favorably. You said that when we Israelites built a temple, you would be pleased to have people worship you there. So as I face this temple {to acknowledge you} as I pray, please answer my prayer.

When I pray to you, or when Israelite people pray to you, we will face this temple {to acknowledge you}. You will be faraway in heaven where you live, but please do what we ask and forgive us {for the sins that we have committed}.

Suppose one person accuses another person of doing something wrong to him. Suppose the first person makes the other person stand in front of your altar outside this temple and swear, ‘I did not do that. May God punish me if I am not telling the truth!’

In that case, please pay attention in heaven and decide which of these people is telling the truth. Then punish the person who is guilty with the punishment that he deserves, and reward the person who is innocent for having done what is right.

Suppose that the enemies of your Israelite people defeat their army in a battle because the Israelites have sinned against you. And suppose that the Israelites then admit that they have done wrong by sinning and that you are right to punish them for sinning. Suppose they stop acting in a sinful way. And suppose they face in the direction of this temple {to acknowledge you} and plead with you to help them.

In that case, please pay attention in heaven, and please forgive your Israelite people for the sins that they have committed. Bring back to this land that you gave to our ancestors any prisoners whom the enemy army may have captured and taken away.

Suppose that your Israelite people sin against you and, to punish them, you do not allow any rain to fall from the sky. Suppose that, because you are punishing them in this way, they face in the direction of this temple {to acknowledge you}, and they pray. Suppose that they admit that you are right to punish them for sinning. Suppose they stop acting in a sinful way.

In that case, {by not allowing rain to fall,} you would have taught them that they needed to live differently. So then please pay attention in heaven to their prayer, and forgive your Israelite people for the sins they have committed. Then send rain on this land that you have decided will belong permanently to your people.

Suppose the people of Israel are not able to grow enough food to eat. Or suppose a deadly disease spreads among the people. Or suppose blight or mildew ruin their crops or locusts or grasshoppers eat up their crops. Or suppose a person is in great distress because an enemy army has surrounded the city where he lives and is attacking it. Or suppose a person gets sick, or many people get sick.

And suppose an Israelite person recognizes that he is suffering because you are correcting him for sinning. Suppose such a person pleads with you to help him. Suppose he stretches out his hands toward this temple {to acknowledge you}.

In that case, please pay attention to his prayer in heaven where you live. If he is truly sorry, forgive him and help him. You are the only one who knows whether a person is truly sorry. So act toward each person as he deserves.
Do this so that the Israelites will deeply respect you and obey you throughout their lives as they live in this land that you gave to our ancestors.

Suppose a foreigner who does not belong to your Israelite people comes from a faraway country because he has heard what a great God you are and what powerful things you have done for your people. Foreigners may come to this temple to {worship you and} pray to you.

In that case, please pay attention to their prayers in heaven where you live. Do for them what they ask you to do. Do that so that all the people groups in the world will know how great you are and revere you as we, your Israelite people, do. Then people throughout the world will know that you are truly present in this temple that I have built.

Suppose that you command your people to go and fight against one of their enemies. And suppose that the Israelite soldiers pray to you {for help}. Suppose that{, to acknowledge you,} they face in the direction of this city of Jerusalem, which you have chosen as the place for this temple that I have built where we Israelites can worship you.
In that case, please pay attention in heaven to their prayers for help, and enable them to defeat their enemies.

Suppose that your people sin against you, as everyone unfortunately does, and you become angry with them. Suppose that {to punish them} you allow one of their enemies to defeat them and take many of them away as prisoners to their own country, perhaps even to a country that is far away.

And suppose that, while your people are in that country to which their enemy took them as captives, they sincerely repent. Suppose they plead with you there and say, ‘We confess that we have sinned by doing very wicked things.’

Suppose that they start obeying you entirely again while they are still in the land of the enemy who captured them. Suppose that they pray to you for help while {to acknowledge you} they face in the direction of this land that you gave to our ancestors. Suppose they face this city of Jerusalem, which you have chosen as the place for this temple that I have built where we Israelites can worship you.
In that case, please pay attention to their prayers for help in heaven where you live, and please rescue them. Please forgive them for the sins that they committed against you.
Oh my God, please regard us favorably and pay careful attention when we pray to you in this place.

Yahweh our God, please come and stay in this place with the sacred chest through which you have acted so powerfully. Yahweh God, may your priests live holy lives so that they can help the people who are faithful to you experience good things that make them rejoice.
Yahweh God, please always help me, the king whom you have appointed. Please remember how you promised King David, who served you well, that you would always love him faithfully.”
When Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from the sky. It burned up the animals that the people had sacrificed and the other offerings. Yahweh’s glory filled the temple.
Because Yahweh’s glory had filled the temple, the priests could not go inside it.

The Israelite people who were there saw the fire coming down and Yahweh’s glory over the temple. They bowed down with their faces touching the stone pavement. They worshiped and thanked Yahweh, saying, “He always does good things for us, and he will faithfully love us forever!”

Then King Solomon and all the Israelites who had come to Jerusalem for the temple dedication offered sacrifices to Yahweh. They sacrificed 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep as fellowship sacrifices to Yahweh. The king and all the Israelites who were there did that to dedicate God’s temple.

The priests stood in their regular positions. The Levites took their places with the musical instruments that King David had made for praising Yahweh. (David had played those instruments himself to praise Yahweh.) They sang, “He loves us faithfully forever!”

The bronze altar that Solomon had made was not large enough for all of the sacrifices that the priests would burn completely that day. It also could not hold all the grain offerings and the fat from the fellowship sacrifices. So Solomon made the middle part of the courtyard, in front of the temple, a holy place for that day. That was where the priests burned sacrifices completely and burned the fat from the fellowship sacrifices.

Solomon and all the Israelites who had come to Jerusalem then celebrated the Festival of Shelters. They celebrated it for seven days. There was a huge crowd of people there who came from many different places in the land of Israel.

On the day after the Festival of Shelters ended, they all gathered together again to worship Yahweh. They had celebrated the dedication of the temple for seven days and the Festival of Shelters for seven days.

The day after that, Solomon told the people they could go back to their homes. (By then it was the 23rd day of the seventh month of their year.) As the people went home, they were very happy because of the good things that Yahweh had done for David and Solomon and the Israelite people, who belonged to him.
After Solomon’s workers had finished building everything that Solomon wanted them to build for the temple and for his royal palace just as he wanted it,

Yahweh appeared to him {in a dream} one night. Yahweh told him, “I agree to do what you asked me to do when you prayed to me. I have made this temple a place where I will be present in a special way so that people can always worship me there.

Suppose that{, to punish the Israelites for sinning,} I do not allow any rain to fall from the sky. Or suppose that I allow locusts to eat up your crops. Or suppose that I allow a deadly disease to spread among the Israelites.

But suppose that the Israelites, who belong to me, become very sorry for their sins and stop sinning. Suppose they ask me to forgive them and they try to do what pleases me. Then I, in heaven, will pay attention to what they ask. I will forgive their sins, and I will make it rain again or stop the locusts from eating their crops or prevent the disease from spreading further.
Then I will regard them favorably, and I will pay careful attention when they pray to me in this place.

I will make the temple you have built a place where I will be always present in a special way. I will always pay attention to what people pray when they face the temple, and I will always care deeply about what happens there.
And as for you, conduct your life as I want you to, just as your father David did. Obey very sincerely all the laws that I have commanded you to obey {as an Israelite}. If you do that,
then I will make sure that you and your descendants are kings of Israel. That is the promise I made to your father David. I told him that one of his descendants would always rule Israel.

But suppose that you or one of your descendants who becomes king stops worshiping me. Suppose you disobey the laws that I have given to you to obey. Suppose that you start to live as people live who worship other gods. Suppose you even bow down to idols that represent those gods.

If you do that, then I will allow an enemy to take the Israelite people away from this land that I have given to them. I will also allow an enemy to destroy this temple that I have made a place where I will be especially present. Then people throughout the world will use the Israelites as an example of a very bad thing happening to a nation. They will even mock other people by saying that they are like the Israelites.

People who see this temple now consider it very beautiful. But enemies will destroy it. People will ask, ‘Why did Yahweh allow enemies to take the Israelite people away from this land and destroy this temple?’

Other people will reply, ‘This happened because the Israelite people abandoned Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors worshiped. He was the one who rescued them from slavery in Egypt. But they became loyal to other gods instead. They lived the way people who worship those other gods live. They even bowed down to idols that represented those gods. That is why Yahweh caused them to experience all these disasters.’”
Solomon’s workers spent 20 years building Yahweh’s temple and Solomon’s palace. After that,
his workers rebuilt the cities that King Huram had given to him. Solomon settled Israelites in those cities.
Solomon’s army then attacked the city of Hamath Zobah and captured it.
Then Solomon’s workers built up the city of Tadmor in the desolate area in the southern part of Judah. They also built cities in the region of Hamath where Solomon kept supplies.
They also built up as border fortress cities Upper Beth Horon and Lower Beth Horon. They built strong walls around them that had gates that people could close with metal bars.

They also built up the city of Baalath and all the cities where Solomon kept supplies and the places where he kept his chariots and horses. They also built everything else that Solomon wanted them to build in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and other places where he had royal authority.
There were many people still living in Solomon’s kingdom who were not Israelites. Rather, they were Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

These people were descendants of members of those people groups who remained in the land of Canaan after the Israelites had destroyed most of their groups. The Israelites had not killed their ancestors. It was those people whom Solomon forced to work hard on his building projects. The Israelites still require those people to work for them.

But Solomon did not force any Israelite people to work hard on his building projects. Instead, some of them became his soldiers, army officers, and leaders of his chariot forces and troops who rode on horses.
King Solomon also had 250 officials who supervised the men who commanded the workers whom he forced to build all those places.

One of Solomon’s wives was a daughter of the king of Egypt. She had been living in the part of Jerusalem that people call the City of David. But Solomon built a palace for her in another part of Jerusalem. He felt that because she was a foreigner, she should not live in a place where the sacred chest had been {before he moved it to the temple}. When David was the king of Israel, he had set up a special tent for the chest on the grounds of his palace, and Solomon felt that this made those grounds holy. So he moved his wife to another place.
Then Solomon offered sacrifices to Yahweh that the priests burned completely on the altar that he had built for Yahweh. That altar was in front of the temple porch.

He did that to obey what Moses had commanded regarding what sacrifices the Israelites should offer at various times. Those times included Sabbath days, New Moon festivals, and the feasts that the law commanded the Israelites to celebrate three times each year. Those were the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Celebration of Weeks, and the Festival of Shelters.

As his father David had instructed, Solomon appointed the groups of priests to do their work. He also appointed the groups of Levites to sing to praise Yahweh and to assist the priests in their daily work. He also appointed groups of Levites to guard each of the gates of the temple. That was what David, that godly man, had commanded.
The people obeyed everything that the king had commanded about the priests and Levites, including his command that they should take care of the temple storerooms.

Solomon’s workers accomplished everything Solomon told them to do to build Yahweh’s temple, from laying its foundation to finishing its last details. And so they completed the construction of Yahweh’s temple.
Then Solomon sent some of his men to the cities of Ezion Geber and Eloth on the coast of the sea in the land of Edom.

Some of King Huram’s subjects knew well how to sail in the ocean. He had them sail some ships to where Solomon’s men were. They sailed together to the region of Ophir. From there, they brought back about 15 metric tons of gold to King Solomon.

The queen who ruled the land of Sheba heard that Solomon had great understanding. She wanted to know whether what she had heard about him was true. So she traveled to Jerusalem to ask him many difficult questions. She brought many of her officials with her in a large caravan. The camels were carrying spices, much gold, and gemstones {as gifts for Solomon}. Solomon welcomed her, and she asked him about everything she wanted to know.
Solomon answered all of her questions. Not one of her questions was too difficult for him to answer.
The Queen recognized that Solomon was very wise. She toured his palace,

and she saw the food that he served. She saw how his many officials sat in different places of honor at meals. She saw how the waiters and cupbearers who served the meals wore splendid uniforms. She also saw the many animals that he brought to the temple for the priests to burn completely as sacrifices. What she saw overwhelmed her.
She told King Solomon, “Everything that I heard back in my own country about how wisely you speak is true!

But I did not believe it was true until I came here and saw it for myself. Indeed, what people told me was only half of what they could have told me about how very wise you are. You are much greater than people told me.
How fortunate are your subjects! And how fortunate are your servants, who are always standing around you and listening to the wise things that you say!

I praise Yahweh, your God, who has shown that he is pleased with you by allowing you to serve him as the king of Israel! Your God loves the Israelite people and wants them always to be a nation. That is why he has appointed you to be a king who will rule them fairly and righteously.”

The Queen of Sheba gave King Solomon {as gifts from what she had brought} over 4, 000 kilograms of gold, many gemstones, and a very large amount of spices. The spices that she gave to Solomon were the best that anyone ever brought to Jerusalem.

The Queen of Sheba admired many things in Jerusalem and asked for them, and King Solomon gave them to her. He gave her more than she had given to him. Then she and the officials who had come with her returned to their own land.
Each year Solomon received over 22 metric tons of gold in tribute from kingdoms that he controlled.

In addition to that, merchants and traders who traveled through and within Israel paid him duties and tolls. Arabian kings also often sent him gifts of gold and silver, and the district governors submitted the taxes they collected in gold or silver.

King Solomon told his workers to take gold and hammer it {into thin sheets and cover} 200 large shields with {those thin sheets of} gold. They used nearly seven kilograms of gold to make each large shield.

He also told his workers to cover 300 smaller shields with gold. They covered each of them with about one and a half kilograms of gold. King Solomon put all of those shields in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
He also had his workers make a large throne for him. The workers inlaid this throne with ivory, and they framed the ivory with borders of very fine gold.
There were six steps in front of the throne. The workers attached a gold footstool to the throne. There was an armrest on each side of the throne. There was a statue of a lion next to each armrest.
There was also a statue of a lion on both sides of each step. So altogether there were 12 statues of lions. There was no throne like this one in any other kingdom.

King Solomon and his court officials drank only from gold cups. His craftsmen also made all of the dishes for the House of the Forest of Lebanon by hammering out gold. (Silver was so common during the time when Solomon ruled that people did not consider it to be valuable.)

They had so much gold because King Solomon had a fleet of ships that were able to sail out on the sea. King Huram’s men sailed them. The ships would sail to many different ports for three years. At the end of that time, they would bring back gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks.
King Solomon became the richest and wisest king in the world.
Kings from many different places came and listened to the wise things that Solomon said about matters that God had enabled him to understand.
Each of the people who came to him brought presents. They brought articles made from silver or gold, or robes, or weapons, or spices, or horses, or mules. The people continued to do this every year.

Solomon had 4,000 stalls where he kept the horses that pulled his chariots. He had 12,000 soldiers who rode on horses. Solomon had built special cities in which to keep chariots, and he kept many of his chariots in them. But he also kept some chariots with him in Jerusalem.
Solomon became the ruler of all the kings in the area from the Euphrates River {in the northeast} to the region of Philistia {in the west} and to the border of Egypt {in the south}.

During the years that Solomon was king, silver became very common in Jerusalem, just as stones are common. Cedar wood became very plentiful, just as the wood is plentiful that comes from the sycamore trees that grow in the foothills of Judah.
Solomon’s purchasing agents would go to Egypt and to many other countries to buy horses for him.

Several books record further things that Solomon did throughout his reign. These books include the records of the prophets Nathan and Ahijah the Shilonite and the accounts by the prophet Iddo of the visions that he saw regarding Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all of Israel for forty years.
Then Solomon died. The Israelites buried him in the part of Jerusalem that people called the City of David. David had been his father. Solomon’s son Rehoboam became the next king.
Leaders from all the tribes of Israel went to the city of Shechem in order to appoint Rehoboam as their king. So Rehoboam also went there.
Jeroboam son of Nebat had fled to Egypt to escape from King Solomon. But when he learned that Solomon had died, he came back from Egypt.
The Israelite leaders asked Jeroboam to come to Shechem, and they went there together to speak with Rehoboam. They told him,
“Your father Solomon forced us to work very hard, but if you allow us to work less hard and allow us to pay fewer taxes, then we will agree to be your subjects.”
Rehoboam replied, “Go away for a couple of days {to give me some time to consider that}. Then come back {and I will give you my answer}.” So those leaders and Jeroboam left.

Then King Rehoboam asked for advice from the older men who had been officials of his father Solomon while he was still living. He asked them, “What do you think I should say in response to what these Israelite leaders have asked me to do?”
They replied, “We recommend that you be kind to them and treat them favorably. If you speak kindly to them when you reply to them, they will always be your loyal subjects.”
But Rehoboam decided not to do what the older men had advised him to do. Instead, he asked for advice from the younger men who had been his friends since they were boys and who were now his advisors.
He asked them, “What do you think we should say in response to these Israelite leaders who have asked me to allow them to work less hard than my father required them to work?”

Those young men who were his boyhood friends replied, “This is what you should tell these people who asked you to allow them to work less hard than your father required them to work. You should say, ‘I am a harsher man than my father was.

This is my answer to you. My father required you to work hard. But I am going to make you work even harder. My father had his overseers discipline you Israelite workers harshly. But I am going to have them discipline you even more harshly.’”
A couple of days after Jeroboam and the Israelite leaders first met with Rehoboam, they came to speak with him again, just as he had told them to do.
The king disregarded the advice that the older men had given him. Instead, he spoke roughly to the Israelite leaders.

He told them what the younger men had advised him to say. He said, “I am going to make you work even harder than my father required you to work. My father had his overseers discipline you Israelite workers harshly. But I am going to have them discipline you even more harshly.”

So the king did not do what the Israelite leaders wanted him to do. That was because God caused him to refuse their request. In that way, Yahweh made happen what he had told Jeroboam son of Nebat through the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite.

When the Israelite leaders realized that Rehoboam was not going to do what they had asked, they responded to him by shouting, “We do not want to be subjects of this descendant of King David! We will not accept this grandson of Jesse as our ruler! We Israelites should all go home! As for this descendant of David, he can rule his own tribe!”
(After that, the only Israelites who accepted Rehoboam as their king were the members of the tribe of Judah.)

King Rehoboam had an official whose name was Hadoram. He supervised the men whom Rehoboam forced to work for him. {Before the Israelite leaders left,} King Rehoboam sent Hadoram out {to try to make them obey him}. But the Israelite people killed him by throwing stones at him. When that happened, King Rehoboam got into his chariot as fast as he could and escaped to Jerusalem.
Ever since that time, the people of the northern tribes of Israel have refused to be subjects of descendants of King David.

When Rehoboam got back to Jerusalem, he gathered 180,000 of the best soldiers from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. He wanted them to fight against soldiers of the northern Israelite tribes {and defeat them} so that he could rule all of the Israelite tribes again.
But Yahweh spoke to the prophet Shemaiah and told him,
“Here is something that I want you to tell Rehoboam son of Solomon, the king of Judah, and all the Israelite people of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

Tell them that I say that they must not go to fight against their fellow Israelites. They must all go home. Tell them that this has happened because I wanted it to happen.” {So Shemaiah went and told that to them,} and they all obeyed what Yahweh had commanded them to do. They did not attack the other Israelites.
Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and he had his workers build walls around several cities in Judah.
They built walls around Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,
Beth Zur, Soko, Adullam,
Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,
Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. All of these cities around which the workers built walls were within the territory of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.
Once these cities had strong walls around them, Rehoboam appointed an army commander in each one. He gave them supplies of food, olive oil, and wine.

He provided large shields and spears for soldiers to use in each of those cities. These arrangements made the cities very difficult to conquer. So Rehoboam continued to rule the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.
Priests and Levites who lived in many places throughout Israel came to Rehoboam and asked to work in his kingdom.

Those descendants of Levi abandoned their property and their pastureland and moved to Jerusalem and to other places in Judah. They did that because Jeroboam{, who had become the king of the other tribes,} and his sons would not let them lead or support the worship of Yahweh.

Instead, Jeroboam appointed priests {other than the ones the law of Moses allowed}. He had them lead worship at hilltop shrines and at places where people adored the goat idols and calf statues that he had made.)
Then people from every tribe in Israel who wanted to worship Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, came to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices to Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.

This made the kingdom of Judah strong, and it made Rehoboam son of Solomon a powerful king, for the next three years. That was because, during that time, the people of his kingdom faithfully worshiped Yahweh as David and Solomon had.
Rehoboam married a woman whose name was Mahalath. She was the daughter of David’s son Jerimoth. Her mother was Abihail, the daughter of Eliab and granddaughter of Jesse.
Rehoboam and Mahalath had three sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
Later Rehoboam married Maacah, the daughter of Absalom, and they had four sons: Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
Rehoboam loved Maacah more than he loved any other of his wives or concubines. Altogether he had 18 wives and 60 concubines, and with them he had 28 sons and 60 daughters.
Rehoboam appointed Maacah’s son Abijah to be the crown prince among his older and younger brothers. He did that because he wanted Abijah to be the next king.

Rehoboam wisely sent some of his other sons to various cities that had walls around them within the territories of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. He made sure that these cities had plenty of supplies. He arranged marriages for each of those sons.
But once Rehoboam had become a secure and powerful king, he and other people in Judah stopped obeying Yahweh’s laws.
As a result, after Rehoboam had been king for almost five years, Shishak, the king of Egypt, came with his army to attack Jerusalem. That happened because the Judeans were no longer loyal to Yahweh.
Shishak brought 1,200 chariots and 60,000 soldiers who rode horses. He also brought more Libyan, Sukkite, and Cushite troops with him from Egypt than anyone could count.
They captured the other cities in Judah that had walls around them. Then they started attacking Jerusalem.

Many Judean leaders had fled to Jerusalem because they were afraid of Shishak and his army. The prophet Shemaiah came and said to them and to King Rehoboam, “Yahweh says that because you have abandoned him, now he is abandoning you. He is going to allow Shishak and his army to capture you.”
Then the king and the other Israelite leaders became very sorry for what they had done. They admitted, “What Yahweh is doing to us is fair.”

When Yahweh recognized that they were sorry for what they had done, he gave another message to Shemaiah. He told him, “Because they are sorry, I will not destroy them. I will allow some Judeans to survive. I will not use Shishak’s army to destroy the people of Jerusalem, even though they have made me very angry.
However, they will become Shishak’s subjects. Then the Judeans will learn that it is much better to serve me than to serve the kings of other countries.”

When King Shishak of Egypt came with his soldiers to attack Jerusalem{, he defeated the Judeans, and then} his soldiers took away the valuable things they found in Yahweh’s temple and in the royal palace. They also took many other valuable things that they found. Because they took the gold shields that Solomon’s workers had made,
King Rehoboam had his workers make bronze shields to replace them. He had the officers of the soldiers who guarded the entrance to his palace take care of these shields.
Whenever the king was going to come into the temple, those guards got those shields and held them, and {after he left the temple,} they returned the shields to their storeroom.

Because Rehoboam was sorry for what he had done, Yahweh stopped being angry with him. He allowed him to continue being the king, even though he was now much weaker. {Yahweh was also merciful because he recognized that} many people in Judah were still living as he wanted them to live.

King Rehoboam made himself a strong king once again in Jerusalem. He had been 41 years old when he became the king, and he ruled for 17 years in Jerusalem. That was the city that Yahweh chose from all the tribes in Israel as the place where people would worship him. Rehoboam’s mother was a woman whose name was Naamah. She was from the nation of Ammon.
Rehoboam did not try to find out what Yahweh wanted him to do, so he did things that were wrong.

Some books record further things that Rehoboam did throughout his reign. These books include the records of the prophet Shemaiah and the records that the prophet Iddo maintained to preserve a register of the descendants of David. The armies of Rehoboam and Jeroboam were continually fighting each other.
When Rehoboam died, people buried him in the part of Jerusalem that they called the City of David. His son Abijah became the next king.
After Jeroboam had been ruling Israel for almost 18 years, Abijah became the king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for three years. His mother was a woman whose name was Micaiah. She was the daughter of Uriel from the city of Gibeah.
Abijah led an army of 400,000 of his best soldiers into battle. Jeroboam formed a battle line of 800,000 of his best and bravest soldiers to oppose him.
Abijah went up on the top of Mount Zemaraim, which is in the hilly area where the descendants of Ephraim lived. He shouted, “Listen to me, Jeroboam and all you Israelite soldiers!
You know well that Yahweh, the God of us Israelites, promised David that he and his descendants would always rule Israel. He made that as a permanent promise.
But Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had been an official of Solomon son of David, rebelled against his king.

That was when Rehoboam son of Solomon {had become king but} was still young and lacked experience. A group of worthless, evil men gathered around Jeroboam, and together they rebelled against him. He was not strong enough to oppose them.

And now you have decided to fight against the kingdom that Yahweh wants David’s descendants to govern. You have a huge army, and you have brought with you the golden statues of calves that Jeroboam has made to be your gods.

But you have driven out the priests whom Yahweh appointed, who are descendants of Aaron. You have also driven out the Levites. You have chosen your own priests, as the people of other countries do. If someone wants to be a priest, all he has to do is sacrifice a young bull and seven rams. Then you let him be a priest. But he is a priest for idols that are not gods at all!
As for us, Yahweh is our God, and we have remained loyal to him. Our priests who serve Yahweh are descendants of Aaron, and the ones who assist them in their work are descendants of Levi.

Every morning and every evening, they burn animals completely on the altar as sacrifices to Yahweh. They burn fragrant incense with them. Every week they place fresh bread in rows on the pure gold table {in Yahweh’s temple}. Every evening they light the lamps that are on the gold lampstand. So we are obeying what Yahweh our God has instructed us to do. But you no longer worship him.

You can see our priests with their trumpets at the front of our army. God is with them. They will blow their trumpets to signal our soldiers to start fighting. {When they do,} you Israelite soldiers should surrender, because you will not be able to defeat Yahweh, the God to whom your ancestors belonged.”

{While Abijah was speaking,} Jeroboam sent some of his soldiers around to attack the army of Judah from the rear. So Jeroboam and many of his soldiers were in front of the army of Judah, but some of his other soldiers were behind them.

The soldiers of Judah looked around and saw that the Israelite solders were going to attack them from the front and from the rear. They cried out to Yahweh for help. Then the priests blew their trumpets
and the soldiers of Judah shouted a loud battle cry. When they did that, God enabled Abijah and the army of Judah to defeat Jeroboam and the army of Israel.
God enabled the army of Judah to win the battle, and the soldiers of Israel fled from the soldiers of Judah.
Abijah and his soldiers won a great victory over them. They killed 500,000 of the best Israelite soldiers.
The soldiers of Judah won the battle because they depended on Yahweh, the God to whom their ancestors belonged. They completely defeated the soldiers of Israel on that occasion.
Abijah’s soldiers chased Jeroboam’s army away, and they captured from the Israelites the cities of Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, and their surrounding villages.
Jeroboam did not become powerful again while Abijah was the king of Judah. Yahweh caused him to become very sick, and he died.
But Abijah became more powerful. He married 14 wives and had 22 sons and 16 daughters.
The record that the prophet Iddo made describes further things that Abijah did. It describes how he lived and things that he said.

When Abijah died, the Judeans buried him in the part of Jerusalem that called the City of David. His son Asa became the next king. While Asa was ruling, the land of Judah was a peaceful place for ten years.
Asa did things that Yahweh his God considered to be good and right.

He had his workers destroy the altars and hilltop shrines for worshiping foreign gods {that his grandfather Rehoboam had built}. He had them smash the stone pillars {that Rehoboam had set up} and cut down the wooden images that represented the goddess Asherah.
Asa told the people of Judah to worship only Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped. He told them to obey the commandments in his law.
He had his workers destroy the idols representing the sun and the hilltop shrines throughout Judah. As a result, while Asa was the king, his kingdom was a peaceful place.
No army attacked Judah during those years, because Yahweh kept them from attacking. This gave Asa the opportunity to build cities with strong walls around them throughout Judah.

Asa told the people of Judah, “We should protect these cities by building strong walls around them that have gates that people can close with metal bars. We should also build defensive towers. This land still belongs to us because we have resolved to worship only Yahweh our God. Because we have done that, he has prevented the enemy countries around us from attacking us.” The people of Judah succeeded in building walls and towers for their cities.

In Asa’s army, there were 300,000 soldiers from the tribe of Judah. Their equipment was large shields and spears. There were also 280,000 men from the tribe of Benjamin. Their equipment was smaller shields and bows and arrows. They were all brave soldiers.
After this, Zerah, the king of the Cushites, attacked Judah with 300 chariots and more soldiers than anyone could count. They marched to the city of Mareshah {southwest of Jerusalem}.
Asa led his army to fight against them. The armies set up battle lines in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

Then Asa prayed out loud to Yahweh his God. He said, “Yahweh, it makes no difference to you whether a kingdom has a large army or a little one. You can help that kingdom either way. We are depending completely on you as our God, Yahweh, and we have come to fight against this huge army for the sake of your reputation. So please help us. Yahweh, you are our God. Do not allow any human force to defeat you.”
Then Yahweh enabled Asa and the Judean army to defeat the Cushite army. Its soldiers ran away,

and Asa and his army pursued them as far as the city of Gerar. Yahweh enabled the Judeans to defeat them severely. So many of the Cushites died that it seemed as if none of them remained alive. The Judeans took away a very great amount of their valuable possessions.

The people who lived in the cities around Gerar became very afraid of Yahweh. As a result, the Judeans were able to conquer all those cities. There were many valuable things in them, and the Judeans took them away.
They also attacked the places where people took care of animals. They took away large flocks of sheep and goats, and they also captured many camels. Then the Judeans went back to Jerusalem.
Then God’s Spirit influenced Azariah son of Oded.

Azariah went to meet Asa. He said to him, “Listen to me, King Asa and all you soldiers from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin! Yahweh will help you when you are loyal to him. If you devote yourselves to him, he will let you have a relationship with him as your God. But if you worship some other god, he will not keep helping you.
For a long time, the Israelites did not worship the true God. They did not have priests teaching them, so they did not obey God’s laws.
But when they experienced trouble, they asked Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, to help them. They devoted themselves to him, and he let them have a relationship with him as their God.
During that time, the people who lived in many countries were experiencing great difficulties, so people were not safe when they traveled.
God was allowing people to experience many difficulties, so the army of one nation would destroy another nation, or the army of one city would destroy another city.
But God will reward you Judeans for what you are doing {to please him}, so you must be strong and not lose courage.

When Asa heard what the prophet {Azariah son of} Oded said when he prophesied, he determined to act. Asa commanded his workers to remove the detestable idols from throughout the territory of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. He also had them remove them from the cities that his soldiers had captured in the hilly area where the descendants of Ephraim lived. Asa also had his workers repair the altar on which priests offered sacrifices to Yahweh that was in front of the entrance to the temple in Jerusalem.

Asa then called for people from throughout the tribes of Judah and Benjamin to come to Jerusalem. Many people from the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon were living among them, and he called them to come too. Those people were there because they had left Israel and moved to Judah when they realized that Yahweh was helping Asa because Asa was loyal to him as his God.
So those people came to Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year that Asa was the king.
At that time, they sacrificed 700 bulls and 7,000 sheep to Yahweh. Those were animals that they had captured when they defeated the Cushite army.
They made a solemn agreement to be wholeheartedly and enthusiastically loyal to Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.
They agreed that they would execute any people who worshiped a different god. It would not matter how important those people were or whether they were men or women.
They said loudly that they would keep this promise to Yahweh. Then people shouted and blew trumpets and ram’s horns {to celebrate}.

The people had made this solemn agreement very sincerely. They had eagerly devoted themselves to Yahweh, and now they had a relationship with him as their God. So people throughout the kingdom of Judah were very happy about this agreement. After this, Yahweh kept the countries around them from attacking them.

King Asa’s grandmother Maacah had been in the influential position of queen mother, but he removed her from that position. He did that because she had made a disgusting wooden statue for the goddess Asherah. Asa had his servants cut down the statue, smash it, and burn it in the Kidron Valley.
He did not order his servants to destroy the shrines for worship on the tops of hills that were in the land of Israel. Even so, Asa was completely faithful to Yahweh for the whole time that he lived.
He ordered his workers to put in God’s temple the silver and gold and other valuable items that he and his father had dedicated.
Asa did not have to fight any more wars until after he had ruled Judah for 35 years.

When Asa had been ruling Judah for almost 36 years, King Baasha of Israel and his army invaded Judah. They captured the city of Ramah {just north of Jerusalem}. Then they started to build a wall around it {so that it would be a border fortress and they could} prevent people from entering or leaving Asa’s kingdom of Judah.

So Asa had his officials collect the silver and golden articles from the storerooms in the temple and his palace. He had them bring those things to Damascus and give them to Ben Hadad, the king who ruled Aram from that city. Asa told his officials to tell Ben Hadad,

“My father had an alliance with your father, and I would like to have an alliance with you. {To make that alliance}, I am giving you this silver and gold. So please break the alliance you have with Baasha, the king of Israel{, and attack him}. That way he will stop invading my kingdom {because he will have to send his army to fight your army}.”

Ben Hadad agreed to do what King Asa wanted. He ordered his army commanders to lead their soldiers to attack some areas in the kingdom of Israel. They attacked the cities of Ijon, Dan, and Abel Maim. They also captured all the cities where the people of the tribe of Naphtali kept their supplies.
When Baasha learned that Ben Hadad’s armies were attacking Israel, he ordered his soldiers to stop building the wall around Ramah.

Then King Asa sent messengers to gather men from throughout the kingdom of Judah. He made the men carry away the stones and timber that Baasha’s soldiers had been using to build a wall around Ramah. With those stones and timber, King Asa had his workers fortify the cities of Geba and Mizpah.

But then the prophet Hanani came to King Asa of Judah and told him, “You should have depended on Yahweh your God, not on the king of Aram You could have defeated the army of the king of Aram, but now you will not.
Remember how the Cushites and Lubites attacked you with a huge army that had very many chariots and soldiers who rode horses. But you depended on Yahweh, and he enabled your army to defeat them.

Yahweh did that because he looks all over the world to see who trusts him completely so that he can help those people powerfully. This time you have acted without regard for Yahweh. So from now on, you will have to fight wars.”

{When he heard that,} Asa became very angry with the prophet. He commanded his officials to put Hanani in prison and clamp a wooden frame around his ankles. He gave that command because he was so angry with Hanani because of what he had said. At that same time, Asa also treated some of his other subjects cruelly.
The book in which the kings of Judah and Israel recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Asa did throughout his reign.

When Asa had been ruling for almost 39 years, he got a disease in his feet. The disease became very severe, but nevertheless he did not ask Yahweh to help him. Instead, he only asked doctors to help him.
Asa died after he had been ruling for about 41 years.

Asa had ordered his workers to carve tombs out of the rocky cliffs near the part of Jerusalem that people called the City of David. The Judeans buried him in one of those tombs. They put his body on a bier that they covered with spices and various ointments that perfumers had prepared. They also lit a huge bonfire to honor him.
Asa’s son Jehoshaphat became the next king of Judah. He built a strong army to defend Judah against attacks from the army of Israel.

He stationed soldiers in all the cities in Judah that had walls around them. He also stationed soldiers to guard other places that were important for defending Judah. He also stationed soldiers in the cities in the territory of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.
Yahweh helped Jehoshaphat because he lived as his father had lived in the first part of his reign. Jehoshaphat did not worship Baal.
Instead, he worshiped the God whom his father had worshiped. He obeyed God’s commands, and he did not do the evil things that the kings of Israel did.
Yahweh enabled him to become completely in control of his kingdom. People from throughout Judah brought gifts to Jehoshaphat. As a result, he became very rich, and people respected him greatly.

He became bold to do what would please Yahweh. He even commanded his workers to destroy the hilltop shrines where people had been worshiping idols. He also commanded them to cut down the wooden images throughout Judah that represented the goddess Asherah.

After Jehoshaphat had been ruling for almost three years, he sent some of his officials to teach the people who lived in various cities in Judah. Those officials were Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah.
He sent Levites and priests to help them. The Levites were Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob Adonijah. The priests were Elishama and Jehoram.
So that they could teach the Judeans, they brought with them a scroll that recorded Yahweh’s law. They went to cities throughout Judah and taught the people who lived in those places.
All the kings who ruled the countries in the area around Judah became very afraid of Yahweh. As a result, they did not attack Jehoshaphat.

Some of the Philistine rulers sent gifts to Jehoshaphat, and they sent silver to him as tribute. The rulers of the nearby Arabian tribes also sent him large numbers of rams and goats that demonstrated their complete submission to him.
Jehoshaphat continued to become a more powerful king. He had his workers build forts and places to store supplies in various locations in Judah.
He did many things to fortify the cities of Judah. He also stationed in Jerusalem many capable soldiers who could fight well.

Soldiers from the same clan fought together. This is how many soldiers were in Jehoshaphat’s army and who their commanders were. Adnah commanded the entire army of Judah, and he directly commanded 300,000 capable soldiers.
Jehohanan was the next highest-ranking officer. He commanded 280,000 other capable soldiers.
Amasiah son of Zichri was the next highest-ranking officer. He volunteered to serve Yahweh in that way. He commanded 200,000 other capable soldiers.
Eliada, who was a great soldier, commanded the army of Benjamin. He directly commanded 200,000 soldiers who used bows and arrows and shields.
The next highest-ranking officer was Jehozabad. He commanded 180,000 men who had weapons for fighting battles.
Jehoshaphat had all of these soldiers available to fight for him, as well as the ones he had stationed in various cities in Judah that had walls around them.
Jehoshaphat had become very rich, and people respected him greatly. But then, to make an alliance with King Ahab of Israel, he arranged for his son Jehoram to marry Ahab’s daughter Athaliah.

A few years later, Jehoshaphat went to visit Ahab at his palace in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered many sheep and cattle to make a feast for him and the officials he had brought with him. {At the feast,} Ahab tried to persuade him to help him recapture Ramoth Gilead.

Finally Ahab asked Jehoshaphat directly, “Will you lead your Judean army and join me as I lead my Israelite army to fight to recapture Ramoth Gilead?” Jehoshaphat replied, “Yes, I will lead my army and join you as you lead your army. My soldiers will fight alongside your soldiers.”
Then Jehoshaphat added, “But we should first ask Yahweh whether we should attack Ramoth Gilead.”
So Ahab summoned his prophets. There were 400 of them. He asked them, “Should I lead my army to fight to recapture Ramoth Gilead, or should I not do that?”
But Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there still a prophet of Yahweh here whom we could ask about this?”

King Ahab replied, “There is still one prophet whom we can ask to tell us what Yahweh says. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, because whenever he prophesies about me, he never says that anything good will happen to me. Instead, he always predicts that bad things will happen to me.”
So King Ahab told one of his officers to summon Micaiah immediately.

Ahab, the king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, were both wearing their royal robes. They were each sitting on thrones in an open square just inside one of the gates in the wall of Samaria. Many prophets were standing in front of them and speaking messages that they said were from God.

One of those prophets was Zedekiah son of Kenaanah. He used iron to make some horns, then he put them on his head and acted like a bull that was goring another animal. He proclaimed to Ahab, “Yahweh. says that your army will keep defeating the Arameans until you have completely destroyed them, just as a bull keeps goring another animal until it has killed it!”
The other prophets who were there said the same thing. They told Ahab, “If you go and attack Ramoth Gilead, you will succeed in conquering it, because Yahweh will enable you to defeat its defenders!”

Meanwhile, the messenger who went to summon Micaiah told him, “Listen to me! All the other prophets are predicting that King Ahab will defeat the Arameans with his army. So be sure that you say the same thing and also predict that he will defeat them.”
But Micaiah replied, “I swear by Yahweh that I will tell Ahab exactly what my God tells me to say.”
When Micaiah came to Ahab, Ahab asked him, “Micaiah, should I lead my army to fight to recapture Ramoth Gilead, or should I not do that?”

But King Ahab {realized that Micaiah did not really mean what he was saying, so he} told Micaiah, “I have told you many times that you must always speak truthfully when you say what Yahweh has revealed to you about me!”

So Micaiah said to him, “{The truth is that in a vision} I saw all the Israelite soldiers had scattered on the hills, the way sheep scatter when they do not have a shepherd. And Yahweh said, ‘Their master is dead. So let them all stop fighting and go home.’”
Then Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “I told you that he never says that anything good will happen to me. Instead, he always predicts that bad things will happen to me!”
Then Micaiah continued, “Let me tell you what Yahweh showed to me! {In a vision} I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne. The angels of heaven were standing on both sides of him.
And Yahweh asked, ‘Who can persuade Ahab to lead his army to attack Ramoth Gilead so that he will die in battle there?’
Finally a spirit came forward and stood in front of Yahweh. It told him, ‘I will deceive him!’
The spirit replied, ‘I will go and inspire all of Ahab’s prophets to tell lies.’
So I am telling you that Yahweh has caused all of your prophets to lie to you. Yahweh has {done that because he has} decided that something terrible is going to happen to you.”
Then Zedekiah walked over to Micaiah and slapped him on his face. He said, “Yahweh’s Spirit has not left me in order to speak to you! That has not really happened!”
Micaiah replied, “You will find out for yourself {to which of us Yahweh’s Spirit has truly spoken} on the day when you hide in the back room of a house!”
King Ahab commanded his soldiers, “Seize Micaiah and take him to Amon, the governor of this city, and to my son Joash.
Tell them that I am commanding them to put this man in prison and give him only a little food to eat and a little water to drink each day until I return safely from the battle.”

Micaiah replied, “If you actually return safely, it will be clear that I was not speaking a message from Yahweh” Then he said to all those who were standing there, “All of you, pay attention to what I have told King Ahab!”
So King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah led their armies to attack Ramoth Gilead.

King Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “When I lead my army into battle, I will wear different clothes {so that no one will recognize that I am the king of Israel}. But you should wear your royal robes.” So Ahab put on different clothes, and they both led their armies into the battle.
The king of Aram had told the men who commanded his chariot forces, “Find the king of Israel and pursue and kill only him. Do not pursue anyone else.”

So when the commanders of the Aramean chariot forces saw Jehoshaphat {wearing his royal robes}, they shouted, “There is the king of Israel!” They started chasing him to attack him. But Jehoshaphat prayed out loud, and Yahweh protected him. He made the commanders stop chasing him.
Those commanders realized that Jehoshaphat was not the king of Israel. So they stopped pursuing him.

But one Aramean soldier shot an arrow at the Israelite soldiers without aiming at anyone in particular. The arrow struck Ahab where the parts of his armor joined together {and so it went through the armor and into his body}. Ahab told the driver of his chariot, “This arrow has wounded me! So turn the chariot around and get me out of the midst of the fighting!”

The Israelites and Arameans fought desperately throughout that day. Ahab’s soldiers helped him keep standing up all day in his chariot facing the Aramean troops. But just as the sun was setting, he died.
But King Jehoshaphat was able to return safely to his palace in Jerusalem.

The prophet Jehu son of Hanani came out of the city to meet him {as he was returning}. He told him, “It was not right for you to help a wicked man or to befriend someone who hated Yahweh. Yahweh is angry with you for doing that.

However, you have also done some good things. After all, you have destroyed the wooden images in your kingdom that represented the goddess Asherah. You have determined that you will worship only the true God.”

Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem. But he left the city again in order to speak with people throughout his kingdom, from the city of Beersheba {in the south} to the hilly area {in the north} where the descendants of Ephraim lived. He got them to worship Yahweh again, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.
He appointed judges in each of the cities throughout the kingdom of Judah that had walls around them. He made sure that each city had its own judges.
He told them, “You will not be judging cases on behalf of people, but on behalf of Yahweh. So make your decisions carefully. Yahweh will help you make the right decisions.

When you judge on behalf of Yahweh our God, you must never acquit guilty people or condemn innocent people. You must never treat some people more favorably than others. You must never take a bribe. So make sure that you revere Yahweh and judge cases honestly.”
After Jehoshaphat returned to Jerusalem, he also appointed some Levites, priests, and leaders of Israelite families to judge cases there according to Yahweh’s laws.
He ordered those judges, “You must revere Yahweh and judge cases honestly and completely sincerely.

Your fellow Israelites who live in other cities will bring you cases that are too difficult for their judges to settle. Some cases will be about whether a person has murdered someone or killed him accidentally. Other cases will deal with various other regulations in the law of Moses. You must warn those Israelites that they must tell the truth throughout the whole trial. If they did not, they would sin against Yahweh, and he would become angry with you and with them. So warn them, and then none of you will become guilty.

I want you to know that Amariah, the high priest, will help you with any matter that relates to the worship of Yahweh and to his laws. Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the leader of the tribe of Judah, will help you with any matter that relates to me and my kingdom. Levites will serve as your court officers. So act courageously! Yahweh will help you if you want to do your work honestly.”
But after he had done these good things, a large army marched to attack Jehoshaphat. Its soldiers were Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites.
