Throughout the land of Israel, they also cut up the idols that represented the sun. Then Josiah returned to Jerusalem.

When Josiah had been ruling for almost 18 years, he decided to do something further to make his kingdom and the temple acceptable places to worship Yahweh. He sent Shaphan son of Azaliah and Maaseiah, the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, his royal secretary, to repair Yahweh’s temple.

They went to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that people had brought to the temple. It was money that the Levites who guarded the entrances to the temple courtyard had collected from people who had come there. They included people from the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim and people who had survived when enemies had conquered the northern kingdom of Israel. They also included people who lived in Jerusalem and other places in the territories of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

Then Hilkiah and his fellow priests gave the money to the men they appointed to supervise the work of repairing the temple. Those supervisors paid the men who did the actual work of repairing and strengthening Yahweh’s temple.

They also gave some of the money to the carpenters and builders to buy stones that workers had shaped and timber for supports and beams for the temple and the buildings around it. The kings of Judah had not cared well for those buildings.

The workers did their work faithfully. The men whom the priests appointed to supervise them included the Levites Jahath and Obadiah, who were descendants of Merari. They also included Zechariah and Meshullam, who were descendants of Kohath. (People respected these Levites who were skillful at playing musical instruments.)
They also supervised the men who carried heavy loads and the foremen of all the crews that did various kinds of work. Other Levites were scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.

One day the priests went to the temple to give the supervisors money that people had brought to the temple. While he was in the temple, the high priest Hilkiah found a scroll that recorded the laws that Yahweh had given to Moses.
So Hilkiah told Shaphan, the king’s secretary, “I have found a scroll in the temple that records the laws that God gave to Moses.” Hilkiah gave the scroll to Shaphan{, and he read it}.
Then Shaphan brought the scroll to King Josiah. He started by giving him a report about the temple repairs. He told him, “I gave the priests all your instructions, and they are obeying them.

They have emptied the chest in which they were collecting money that people brought to the temple. They have given the money to the men who are supervising the work so that they can pay the workers who are repairing the temple.”
Then Shaphan also told the king, “The high priest Hilkiah gave me this scroll.” And Shaphan read to the king what the scroll recorded.
When the king heard the laws that Shaphan was reading to him from the scroll, he tore his robes {to show how concerned he was that Yahweh would punish the Judeans}.
Then King Josiah gave special instructions to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Akbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan his royal secretary, and Asaiah, his special advisor. He told them,

“Now that Hilkiah has found this scroll, I want you to go and ask Yahweh what I and the surviving Israelites and the people of Judah should do about what it says. Our ancestors did not obey Yahweh’s commandments. They should have done everything that this scroll records. So Yahweh must be very angry with us.”

So Hilkiah and the other men whom the king had sent went to consult a woman whose name was Huldah. She was a prophetess, and she lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem. She was the wife of Shallum, whose father was Tikvah and whose grandfather was Harhas. Shallum took care of the garments that the priests wore in the temple. Those five men told Huldah about the scroll that Hilkiah had found.
In response, she told them, “Yahweh, the God whom we Israelites worship, says that he wants you to say something to the man who sent you to me.

Yahweh says that he is going to make something terrible happen to this city and to the people who live here. He is going to make all the bad things happen that the scroll people read to King Josiah describes.

He is going to do that because they stopped worshiping him and burned incense to {honor} other gods. They made many idols, and that has made him very angry. He is so angry with them that he is certainly going punish them.
But there is something further that you are to tell the king of Judah, who sent you to ask Yahweh about what the scroll said. Yahweh, the God whom we Israelites worship, says that

he is going to treat him mercifully. Yahweh will do that because he was so sad and he acted humbly toward him when he heard what Yahweh said he was going to do to punish this city and the people who live here. {When King Josiah heard that,} he acted humbly toward Yahweh, and he tore his robes {to show his distress}, and he wept. He knew that Yahweh was watching him. That is why Yahweh declares {that he is going to treat him mercifully}.

Yahweh wants you to tell Josiah that he is going to allow him to die {before this happens}, and the Judeans will bury him peacefully. Yahweh is still going to cause many terrible things to happen to Jerusalem and the people who live in it. But Josiah will not be alive to see that.” The officials returned to King Josiah and reported what Huldah had told them.
Then King Josiah sent messengers to summon all the elders of Jerusalem and the other places in the kingdom of Judah.

The king went to the temple courtyard. A great crowd of many different kinds of people from Jerusalem and other places in Judah assembled there with him. Many priests and Levites were there along with ordinary people. While they all listened, the king read to them all the laws that the scroll recorded that Yahweh had given the Israelites when he made his solemn agreement with them. Hilkiah had found that scroll in the temple.

The king was standing next to a pillar {on the temple porch}. He made a solemn agreement with Yahweh that he would live as Yahweh wanted him to live. He promised to obey all of Yahweh’s laws wholeheartedly and enthusiastically. In that way, the terms of the solemn agreement that the scroll from the temple described became the law of Israel once again.

King Josiah made the people who had gathered from Judah and Benjamin to the temple courtyard promise to obey that solemn agreement. From then on, the people who lived in Jerusalem {and in the rest of the kingdom} obeyed the solemn agreement that they had made with Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.

Josiah ordered his workers to remove all the disgusting idols from throughout the territory of the Israelites. He commanded everyone who lived in his kingdom to worship only Yahweh as their God. For as long as Josiah was alive, the people did not worship gods other than Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.

Then Josiah arranged for the people to celebrate the Passover Festival in Jerusalem to honor Yahweh. They slaughtered the lambs for the Passover feast on the fourteenth day of the first month {of the year}.
Josiah told the priests to resume the work that they each did at the temple. He encouraged them to do their work well.

The Levites had special work to do for Yahweh, including teaching the Israelites. But they had been carrying the sacred chest around {on poles} on their shoulders {to keep it safe}. But Josiah told them, “You may now put the sacred chest {safely} back in the temple that Solomon son of David built when he was the king of Israel. You may now devote yourselves to serving Yahweh your God and his Israelite people.
Get ready {to help the people celebrate Passover}. When David and his son Solomon were kings of Israel, they wrote instructions for the work that each of your clans should do.

I want each of your clans to stand {in a different part of} the temple area. I am going to have your fellow Israelites who are not priests or Levites gather in the temple area according to their own clans. Part of each of your clans should help one of those family groups.

To provide a Passover feast for your fellow Israelites, kill the animals for the meal. Then wash yourselves {and hand their blood to the priests}. Do what Yahweh told Moses that the Israelites should do.”

Josiah provided 30,000 young sheep and goats from his own flocks. These were enough for the Passover meals for all the Israelites who came for the feast. He also provided 3,000 bulls from his own herds {as fellowship sacrifices}.

His officials also voluntarily contributed animals for the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel were important officials at the temple. They gave 2,600 young sheep and goats to provide Passover meals for the priests. They also gave 300 bulls {for fellowship sacrifices}.

Some of the leaders of the Levites gave 5,000 sheep and goats to provide Passover meals for the Levites. These men were Conaniah, his younger brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad. They also gave 300 bulls {for fellowship sacrifices}.

This is how they arranged for the Passover meal. The priests stood in their places. The Levites gathered in their clans {in order to help various family groups}. That is what the king had commanded them to do.
The Levites killed the Passover lambs and goats and handed their blood {in bowls} to the priests, who sprinkled the blood on the altar. The Levites removed the skins from the animals,

and they also removed the parts of the animals that the priests would burn completely on the altar. They gave those parts to the various family groups that they were assisting. The families then offered those parts to Yahweh in order to obey the instructions that Moses had written in the law. The priests, Levites, and people did the same thing with the oxen.

As the law required, the Levites roasted the meat from the lambs and goats for the Passover meal over an open fire. But they cooked differently the meat from the animals that the king and officials had consecrated for fellowship offerings. They boiled that meat in pots and kettles and pans. The Levites served both kinds of meat immediately to all the people who had come for the feast.

The priests, the descendants of Aaron, were busy for the entire day burning the parts of the animals that belonged to Yahweh, including their fat, completely on the altar. {Since they did not have the opportunity to prepare their own meals,} after the Levites had prepared meals for the people, they prepared meals for themselves and for the priests.

The singers who were descendants of Asaph stayed in the places where King David, Asaph, Heman, and the king’s prophet Jeduthun had commanded them to stand {and sing}. The Levites who guarded each of the gates of the temple courtyard remained at their positions. Their fellow Levites prepared food for them to eat, so the singers and gatekeepers did not need to leave their places.

On that day, the priests, Levites, and people did everything necessary to celebrate the Passover Festival to honor Yahweh. That is what King Josiah had commanded them to do. They also presented offerings that the priests burned completely on Yahweh’s altar.
The Israelites who came for the feast celebrated the Passover on that day, and then they celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

The Israelites had not celebrated a Passover Festival like this one since the time when the prophet Samuel lived. None of the kings of Israel had celebrated the Passover as Josiah did with the priests, the Levites, and the other people of Judah and Israel who came to Jerusalem to celebrate with the people who lived there.
They celebrated this Passover Festival when Josiah had been ruling for almost 18 years.

Josiah did all these things to restore the worship of Yahweh at his temple. Some time later, King Neco of Egypt led his soldiers to fight {the Babylonians} at the city of Carchemish near the Euphrates River. Josiah led his army to fight against them.

Neco sent some messengers to tell Josiah, “I have no quarrel with you, King of Judah. I have not come now to attack you. Instead, I am going to fight against my enemy, the king of Babylon. God has told me to hurry. So stop opposing God, who is helping me. Otherwise, God will kill you.”

But Josiah did not do what Neco told him to do, even though God was speaking through him. He did not return to Jerusalem with his army. But he disguised himself in order to fight against Neco. He led his soldiers to fight against Neco’s army at the plain of Megiddo.
As the Egyptian archers were shooting at the Judean soldiers, one of them hit King Josiah. He told his officers, “I am badly wounded, so take me away from here.”

So they took him out of his war chariot and put him in his traveling chariot. They brought him to Jerusalem, where he died. The Judeans buried him in the royal tombs. People throughout Jerusalem and other places in Judah mourned for him.

The prophet Jeremiah composed a sad song about Josiah because he had died. Many men and women still sing sad songs that tell about Josiah. The Judean leaders gave orders to teach these songs to the people. The collection of laments records them.

The book in which the kings of Israel and Judah recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Josiah did throughout his reign. This includes how he faithfully obeyed Yahweh’s laws, which Moses wrote down.
Then the Judeans appointed Josiah’s son Jehoahaz as the next king in Jerusalem.
Joahaz was 23 years old when he became the king, but he ruled in Jerusalem for only three months.
Then the king of Egypt came and took him away. He also forced the people of Judah to pay him three and one third metric tons of silver and thirty-three kilograms of gold.

The king of Egypt appointed Jehoahaz’s younger brother Eliakim to be the next king of the people who lived in Jerusalem and in other places in Judah. He changed Eliakim’s name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Joahaz to Egypt as his prisoner.
Jehoiakim was 25 years old when he became the king of Judah, and he ruled from Jerusalem for 11 years. He did many things that Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, considered to be evil.
Then the army of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacked Jehoiakim’s army. They captured Jehoiakim, bound him with bronze chains, and took him away to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar’s soldiers also took some of the articles that the priests used in Yahweh’s temple. They brought them to Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar put them in the temple of his god.

The book in which the kings of Israel and Judah recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Jehoiakim did. This includes the disgusting acts he committed and what a bad person he was. His son Jehoiachin became the next king of Judah.
Jehoiachin was 18 years old when he became the king of Judah. He ruled from Jerusalem for only three months and ten days. He did many things that Yahweh considered to be evil.

During the spring of the next year, King Nebuchadnezzar sent soldiers to bring him to Babylon. They also took away many valuable things from Yahweh’s temple. Nebuchadnezzar appointed Jehoiachin’s uncle Zedekiah to rule instead over the people who lived in Jerusalem and in other parts of Judah.
Zedekiah was 21 years old when he became the king, and he ruled from Jerusalem for 11 years.

He did many things that Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, considered to be evil. Yahweh gave the prophet Jeremiah a message to warn him. But when Zedekiah heard that message, he was not sorry for the wrong things he had been doing.

He was very proud, and he was very stubborn. So he did not start obeying Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, once again. King Nebuchadnezzar had made him promise to be loyal to him. He had made him say that he hoped God would punish him if he broke that promise. Even so, Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar.

Most of the leaders of the priests and the people of Judah also did many very wicked things. They did the same kind of disgusting things as the people had done whom Yahweh forced to leave the land of Canaan. Yahweh had made his temple in Jerusalem a special place where he was present. But those leaders put idols in the temple area, so that Yahweh no longer considered it an acceptable place to worship him.

Yahweh was the God whom the ancestors of the people of Judah had worshiped. He wanted to be merciful to his people, and he did not want anyone to destroy his temple. So he continually sent prophets to them with messages to warn them.

But the people laughed at the prophets. They treated God’s messages as if they were not important. They treated the prophets very badly. Finally Yahweh became so angry with his people that he decided he would certainly destroy Judah.

He influenced the king of Babylon to attack Judah with his army. They killed the Judean soldiers with their swords, even those who went to the temple area for safety. They did not spare anyone, regardless of their sex or age. God enabled the army of Nebuchadnezzar to conquer the entire city.

His soldiers took to Babylon all the items of every size that the priests used in God’s temple. They also took the valuable things that were in the storerooms at the temple and the valuable things that belonged to the king and his officials.
They burned the temple, and they broke down the wall around Jerusalem. They burned all the important buildings in Jerusalem, and they destroyed all the valuable things that they did not carry away.

There were some people whom the soldiers had not killed. They took those people away as prisoners to Babylon. Those people had to work for Nebuchadnezzar and the kings who ruled Babylon after him until the army of Persia conquered Babylon.

Those people remained in Babylon for 70 years. During that time, no one planted or harvested crops in their land. As a result, the soil recovered, as if would have done if the people had obeyed the law of Moses and not planted crops every seventh year. Yahweh had said through Jeremiah that this would happen, and it did.

During the first year after Cyrus, king of Persia, {conquered the kingdom of Babylon,} Yahweh motivated Cyrus to write a message. Yahweh did this in order to make something happen that Jeremiah had predicted. Cyrus sent messengers throughout his empire with copies of the message, and he ordered them to proclaim it as they went. This is what they proclaimed:

“I, King Cyrus, rule the Persian Empire, and I say, ‘Yahweh, the God who is in heaven, has made me ruler over the great kingdoms of this part of the world. Now he has assigned me to {make sure that his people} build a temple for him in {the city of} Jerusalem in {the province of} Judah. Any of you who belong to his people may go {to Jerusalem in Judah to rebuild this temple for Yahweh}. And may Yahweh your God help you!’”
